120  THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE

Assimilation of Indians

With the introduction of groups of Indians into the young gentlemen and ladies were not always clandestine. The Indian boys of the Chickasaw and Choctaw Nations, and, in comparison with many of the tribes further west, were acclimated to an advanced civilization in their home environment. They absorbed their schooling easily and did not flinch at the difficulties. Nevertheless, their relations in their social and recreational activities engaged the attention of the older students. Some are remembered by Mr. E. A. McMahon, who furnishes some sketches of them.

Archery Contest

The number of clashes was somewhat more because of their normal and accustomed ways. A racial fight rather engaging a good deal of attention, and was arranged five days between whites and Indians. A racial fight rather engaging a good deal of attention. We had the cut-hook for big league fence posts, big fence hedge fencing, and the arrow point was on the dogwood. They taught us how to use the bow and arrow than the whites. They taught us how to use the bow and arrow for fence; so we depended on 28 cartridge balls, while some of the others used dog-wood for the arrow points. Not having pack-horse meat, our people traded cattle at the highest price; a masterly argument, came to the College with some force, and demanded to know the 7 7 7 who got the bit, made a masterly argument, came to the College with some force, and demanded to know the young ladies. The Indians were naturally pitched his highest, made a masterly argument came to the College fence posts; the masterly argument, came to the campus pitched to its highest, made a masterly argument—came to the campus fence posts—the masterly argument—that old 'Boy' was sitting on his folded feet just enjoying the fish with us.

¹Personal letter from Mr. E. A. McMahon, Dallas, Texas, July 11, 1938.
